transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. Thank you for coming in today. What brings you to the clinic?

Hi, Doctor. Thank you so much for having me. Um... I hope I'm not wasting your time, I really appreciate you seeing me. 

I guess my manager at the warehouse said I had to come in. It's... it's a little embarrassing, honestly. I don't want you to think I'm a bad worker, because I really try to do a good job, but... they said I was doing some strange things on the floor. 

Like, I guess sometimes I'll just sort of freeze with my arms up in the air right by the forklift. And... um... I've been copying the beeping sounds it makes, and mimicking the hand signals. I didn't mean to cause a disruption or anything. I was just moving the boxes in these specific little patterns, you know? But everyone was yelling at me to stop. I really didn't mean to upset anyone, I just got a little caught up, I guess. 

Does that... does that sound like the kind of thing I'm supposed to be here for? I just want to make sure I'm doing what I'm supposed to do to get back to work.

When you freeze with your arms up or make those beeping sounds, do you feel like you have to do it, like it's something you can't stop yourself from doing? Or can you choose to stop if you really try?

Um... honestly, I'm not totally sure. I don't think it's like I *have* to do it... I definitely don't want you to think I'm out of control or anything like that. I'm really not. I guess... I just sort of don't even realize I'm doing it until someone yells my name? 

Like, if I noticed I was doing it, I would absolutely stop right away, I promise. I always want to follow the safety rules on the floor. It's just... I don't really know how to explain it. I'm sorry, I hope that's an okay answer. Does that make sense? I just don't want to sound like I'm doing it on purpose to cause trouble, because I really am trying my best to be a good employee.
Before you freeze up or make those beeping sounds, do you ever feel like there's a buildup or pressure inside you that makes you want to do it? Like an urge or tension that builds up?

Um... no, I don't think so. I definitely don't feel... like, wound up or tense beforehand. I promise I'm not a stressed-out guy or anything, I really try to stay super positive on the floor. 

So, no, there's no pressure or urge building up inside me. It's not like I'm bursting to do it and just can't hold it in. It just... kind of happens, and then I'm doing it without realizing. 

I hope that's a good sign? Like, maybe that means it's not too serious of a problem? I really want to be helpful and give you the right information... did I explain that okay?
When did you first start doing these kinds of things - freezing up, making sounds, or copying movements? Can you remember how old you were when this first started happening?

Um... let me think. I want to make sure I give you the right timeline, so I'm being as helpful as possible. I'm 20 now, and... well, it definitely hasn't been happening my whole life or anything. I've always tried to be a really steady, normal worker. 

I guess... it's been about six months now? Yeah, maybe around six months ago is when the guys at the warehouse started saying my talking was confusing and that I was doing those strange behaviors. I really didn't mean to confuse anyone, I promise. 

It's just been the last half year or so. So it's a pretty recent thing, you know? Not a huge, permanent problem, I hope. I really hope I didn't wait too long to come see you... did I answer that okay? I just want to make sure I'm giving you what you need so I can get back to doing a good job.

Going back further - when you were a little kid, like in elementary school or even younger, did you ever do things like this? Did you have any repetitive movements, sounds, or ways of playing that were unusual or that other kids noticed?

Um... no, definitely not. When I was a kid, I was completely normal. I didn't do anything weird like that. I played just like all the other kids... I always wanted to fit in and be a good kid, you know? 

I never had any strange habits or made weird noises or anything. My teachers always said I was a pleasure to have in class. I promise, I was a really typical kid. I didn't have any problems like this growing up. 

So it's really just been the last six months. Does that... does that help? Like, maybe since it's so new, it's something that can be fixed pretty easily? I just really want to go back to being normal and doing my job well. I hope that's the right answer.

When you're talking with your coworkers or other people, do you ever have trouble understanding what they mean, or do they sometimes say you're hard to understand? Or do you find it difficult to know what to talk about with people?

Um... well, I always try really hard to communicate well with everyone. I want to be friendly and, you know, a good team player! But... I guess sometimes the guys at work do say I'm a little hard to follow. It's not that I don't know what to talk about, I just... maybe I try to share a little too much at once? 

Like, when the supervisor asks me which pallets are going on the truck, I start trying to explain it to him so he has all the information. But then my words just kind of jump around. I'll start on the load sheet, and then somehow it reminds me of my old house, and then fishing, and then church boxes... and by the time I'm done talking, nobody really knows what I meant. 

I really don't mean to confuse anybody, I promise. I just want to give them all the details so I'm doing a thorough job. I hope my supervisor isn't too upset with me about it. I'm really trying to get better at just giving the short answer so I don't hold anyone up. Did... did that make sense? I hope I'm answering your questions the right way.
When you were growing up as a child, did you have any difficulty making friends or playing with other kids? Did other children ever say you were odd or hard to understand?

Um... no, definitely not. I didn't have any trouble like that at all. I was always really good at making friends, I think. I always tried to be nice to everyone and, you know, share and be a good playmate. 

I definitely wasn't the odd kid out... I rode bikes and played with the neighborhood guys just fine. Nobody ever said I was hard to understand back then. I really tried hard to be a good friend and fit in with the group, just like I try to be a good team player at the warehouse now. 

I hope that's... I mean, is it helpful to know that I was completely fine back then? I just want you to know I've always been a pretty normal, friendly guy. I'm really hoping you can help me get back to that. Was that the right kind of information?

When you were in school, did teachers or your parents ever mention concerns about how you understood social situations - like knowing when it was your turn to talk, understanding jokes, or picking up on what people were feeling?

Um... no, definitely not. My parents were always really big on manners, so I always knew to wait my turn and be polite. I never wanted to interrupt anybody or cause any trouble for the teachers. I always tried to be really considerate of how other people were feeling, you know? Like, if someone was upset, I'd try to be nice and help them out. 

And I got jokes just fine... I mean, I always laughed when my friends were laughing so I wouldn't ruin the fun or make things awkward. So, no, nobody ever had any concerns like that. The teachers always said I was really respectful. I was a really good student, I promise. 

Is... is that okay? I hope I'm not repeating myself too much, I just want to make sure you know I really didn't have any problems like this before. I'm trying to be as helpful as I can so I can get back on track. Did I answer that right?
If you really concentrated and tried hard, like if your job depended on it, do you think you could stop yourself from doing those freezing movements or making the beeping sounds while you're at work?

Um... freezing movements? And... beeping sounds? I... I'm not really sure what you mean by that, doctor. I don't think I do anything like that at work. 

I mean, I'm always moving around a lot, lifting boxes and moving pallets and stuff. It's a really physical job, so I'm always trying to stay active and get things done quickly so my supervisor is happy. I definitely wouldn't just freeze up or stop working, especially if my job depended on it! I try really hard to be a good worker. 

And... beeping? Like a machine? I don't make noises like that. Sometimes the forklifts beep when they back up, maybe that's what you're thinking of? I just try to stay quiet and focus on my tasks so I don't bother anyone. 

I really hope I'm not doing something weird that I don't know about... I want to be doing a good job. Did... did someone say I was doing that? I promise I'm really trying my best to be normal at work. Is that... is that the right answer? I just want to make sure I'm giving you the information you need.

I want to make sure I understand - your manager and coworkers at the warehouse, they told you that you were freezing with your arms up and making beeping sounds, correct? Did that actually happen, or do you think they might have misunderstood what you were doing?

Um... well, I guess... I guess maybe they did say something like that. I didn't mean to make it sound like I was lying before, I just... I really want you to think I'm doing a good job. 

But, um, yeah, I suppose that's why they brought me in here. The manager and some of the guys were getting kind of upset. I guess sometimes by the forklift, I... I sort of get stuck with my arms up in the air. And I do make those beeping noises, like the truck backing up, and I copy the hand signals the drivers use. I don't really mean to be disruptive, I promise. It's just... it happens. 

And sometimes I arrange the boxes in, like, these specific little patterns instead of just stacking them how they want. Even when they're yelling at me to stop and hurry up, I just... I keep doing it. I know it probably looks really weird to them. I really try not to be a bother, though. 

I'm sorry I didn't just say that a minute ago. I just felt really embarrassed about it. I want to be a good worker and not cause problems. Is... is it okay that I told you that now? I hope you're not mad at me for not being clear right away. I'm really trying to be helpful, doctor.

When you're about to freeze up with your arms in the air or make those beeping sounds, do you get any kind of warning feeling first - like an itch, a tingling, a buildup of tension, or anything uncomfortable that makes you feel like you need to do it?

Um... no, I don't think I feel anything like that. There's no... no itch or tingling or tension or anything. It's not like I feel uncomfortable and need to do it. It just... it just sort of happens before I even really realize I'm doing it. 

I'm really sorry, I wish I could tell you there was a warning feeling. If there was, maybe I could catch myself and stop it so I wouldn't bother my manager or the other guys at the warehouse. I really do want to just do my work normally and be a good employee. 

Is... is it bad that I don't feel it coming on? I hope I'm giving you the right information. I'm really trying to pay close attention to everything you're asking, I just... I really don't notice anything before it starts. Did... did I answer that okay?

Besides the freezing movements and beeping sounds at work, do you have any other things you really like to do over and over - like collecting things, organizing things in specific ways, or activities you get really focused on that are hard to stop once you start?

Um... no, not really. I don't... I don't collect anything or do things over and over like that. I just like to keep things neat, you know? Like... just normal organizing. I don't get stuck doing it or anything. 

I mean, I mentioned the boxes before, but that's just because I want the warehouse to look nice and tidy for the manager. I'm not... I'm not obsessed with it or anything weird like that. I just want to do a good job. 

I really try to just go to work, do what I'm supposed to do, and then go home and relax. I don't have any strange hobbies or anything. I just try to be a normal guy. Is... is that what you were asking? I hope I'm explaining things right. I really want to make sure I'm giving you good answers.

When you're doing those things - like freezing with your arms up or making the beeping sounds - are you aware that you're doing them while they're happening, or do you only realize after someone points it out to you?

Um... well, it's kind of hard to explain. I guess... I guess I sort of know I'm doing it while it's happening, but it's not like I'm thinking about it on purpose. It's more like... I'm just doing it, and I know I'm doing it, but I don't really think about how it looks until someone yells at me. 

I mean, I'm not totally checked out or anything like that. I'm still there. I just... I get kind of caught up in it, I suppose. But I'm definitely awake and aware. I don't want you to think I'm losing my mind or blacking out or anything scary like that. I'm just... I'm just doing my own thing for a minute. 

Is that... does that make sense? I hope I'm not making it sound worse than it is. I really am aware of my surroundings, I promise. I just want to make sure I'm giving you the right answer. Did I explain that okay?

Besides the beeping sounds you make like the forklift - are there any other sounds or words that just come out of your mouth that you don't plan to say? Like throat clearing, grunting, or words that just pop out?

Um... no, no other sounds. Just... just the beeping. I definitely don't grunt or clear my throat weirdly or... or blurt things out. I'm not... I'm not doing anything disruptive like that. 

I really try to keep quiet while I'm working, except for when I'm, you know, doing the forklift thing. I know it's important to be professional, even in a warehouse. I wouldn't want to make any noises that would make people uncomfortable or think I'm being rude. 

I'm pretty good at controlling what I say, I think. I don't just have words popping out. I hope... I hope that's a good thing? Like, it means I'm mostly doing okay, right? I'm really trying to give you the whole picture so you can see I'm trying my best. Is... is that the kind of answer you needed?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the patient has trouble communicating with coworkers or if others find the patient hard to understand, which directly addresses the disorganized thinking and speech symptom.

patient.answer:
Um... well, I always try really hard to communicate well with everyone. I want to be friendly and, you know, a good team player! But... I guess sometimes the guys at work do say I'm a little hard to follow. It's not that I don't know what to talk about, I just... maybe I try to share a little too much at once? 

Like, when the supervisor asks me which pallets are going on the truck, I start trying to explain it to him so he has all the information. But then my words just kind of jump around. I'll start on the load sheet, and then somehow it reminds me of my old house, and then fishing, and then church boxes... and by the time I'm done talking, nobody really knows what I meant. 

I really don't mean to confuse anybody, I promise. I just want to give them all the details so I'm doing a thorough job. I hope my supervisor isn't too upset with me about it. I'm really trying to get better at just giving the short answer so I don't hold anyone up. Did... did that make sense? I hope I'm answering your questions the right way.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient has shown early developmental differences in social communication and interaction (characteristic of autism spectrum disorder) versus acquired behavioral changes without developmental history (more consistent with other tic disorders). This is the key differentiator between F84.5 (Autism Spectrum Disorder) and F95.9 (Unspecified Tic Disorder).
doctor.question: When you were growing up as a child, did you have any difficulty making friends or playing with other kids? Did other children ever say you were odd or hard to understand?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about childhood social interactions, making friends, and whether the patient was considered odd or hard to understand as a child. This relates to neurodevelopmental history (like autism spectrum traits or childhood onset schizophrenia), which is not covered by any of the provided symptom profiles (Disorganized Thinking, Disorganized Behavior, Functional Impairment, Duration, Psychotic Symptoms Duration).

patient.answer:
Um... no, definitely not. I didn't have any trouble like that at all. I was always really good at making friends, I think. I always tried to be nice to everyone and, you know, share and be a good playmate. 

I definitely wasn't the odd kid out... I rode bikes and played with the neighborhood guys just fine. Nobody ever said I was hard to understand back then. I really tried hard to be a good friend and fit in with the group, just like I try to be a good team player at the warehouse now. 

I hope that's... I mean, is it helpful to know that I was completely fine back then? I just want you to know I've always been a pretty normal, friendly guy. I'm really hoping you can help me get back to that. Was that the right kind of information?

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient has a lifelong pattern of social/communication difficulties (suggesting autism spectrum disorder) versus acute onset of only motor/vocal tics (suggesting tic disorder). The key differentiator is whether there's evidence of developmental social communication impairment in childhood that predates the current tic-like behaviors.
doctor.question: When you were in school, did teachers or your parents ever mention concerns about how you understood social situations - like knowing when it was your turn to talk, understanding jokes, or picking up on what people were feeling?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about childhood social development, specifically regarding social cues, pragmatics of speech, understanding jokes, and empathy (often exploring autism spectrum traits). The patient's symptom profile does not contain an item addressing childhood social development or understanding of social situations.

patient.answer:
Um... no, definitely not. My parents were always really big on manners, so I always knew to wait my turn and be polite. I never wanted to interrupt anybody or cause any trouble for the teachers. I always tried to be really considerate of how other people were feeling, you know? Like, if someone was upset, I'd try to be nice and help them out. 

And I got jokes just fine... I mean, I always laughed when my friends were laughing so I wouldn't ruin the fun or make things awkward. So, no, nobody ever had any concerns like that. The teachers always said I was really respectful. I was a really good student, I promise. 

Is... is that okay? I hope I'm not repeating myself too much, I just want to make sure you know I really didn't have any problems like this before. I'm trying to be as helpful as I can so I can get back on track. Did I answer that right?

inference.note: Ruled out F84.5 (Autism Spectrum Disorder). Patient reports normal childhood social development, no early difficulties with social interaction or communication, no repetitive behaviors in childhood. Current symptoms (echolalia, echokinesia, freezing) began only 6 months ago in adulthood, inconsistent with autism which manifests in early development. Remaining diagnosis is Unspecified Tic Disorder (F95.9), which better fits the acute onset of involuntary motor and vocal tics without premonitory urges.

doctor.intent: Determine if these are involuntary tics (which would support F95.9 - Unspecified Tic Disorder) versus voluntary mimicry or echolalia, by asking about the patient's ability to suppress the behaviors with effort and awareness.
doctor.question: If you really concentrated and tried hard, like if your job depended on it, do you think you could stop yourself from doing those freezing movements or making the beeping sounds while you're at work?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the patient's ability to consciously control or stop the disorganized/abnormal behaviors (freezing, beeping sounds) if they tried hard. The S022 profile describes the manifestation of these behaviors but does not specify whether the patient has voluntary control over them or can suppress them with concentration. Therefore, there is no direct match in the provided symptom profiles.

patient.answer:
Um... freezing movements? And... beeping sounds? I... I'm not really sure what you mean by that, doctor. I don't think I do anything like that at work. 

I mean, I'm always moving around a lot, lifting boxes and moving pallets and stuff. It's a really physical job, so I'm always trying to stay active and get things done quickly so my supervisor is happy. I definitely wouldn't just freeze up or stop working, especially if my job depended on it! I try really hard to be a good worker. 

And... beeping? Like a machine? I don't make noises like that. Sometimes the forklifts beep when they back up, maybe that's what you're thinking of? I just try to stay quiet and focus on my tasks so I don't bother anyone. 

I really hope I'm not doing something weird that I don't know about... I want to be doing a good job. Did... did someone say I was doing that? I promise I'm really trying my best to be normal at work. Is that... is that the right answer? I just want to make sure I'm giving you the information you need.

inference.note: Patient now denies the freezing and beeping behaviors that were initially reported, suggesting possible factitious presentation or exaggeration. However, the combination of recent-onset repetitive behaviors (6 months), flight of ideas/tangential speech, social awkwardness despite claiming normalcy, and lack of childhood history could suggest an emerging neurodevelopmental or neuropsychiatric condition. Added F84.9 (Autism Spectrum Disorder, unspecified) as differential given speech patterns and social difficulties, though patient denies childhood symptoms.

doctor.intent: Clarify whether the patient has insight into their own behaviors - do they actually deny the freezing/beeping behaviors occurred, or are they minimizing/downplaying them due to anxiety about judgment? This is crucial to differentiate between F95.9 (Tic Disorder) where behaviors are often ego-syntonic or not fully recognized, versus F84.9 (Autism Spectrum Disorder) where the patient would typically have better awareness of their own actions.
doctor.question: I want to make sure I understand - your manager and coworkers at the warehouse, they told you that you were freezing with your arms up and making beeping sounds, correct? Did that actually happen, or do you think they might have misunderstood what you were doing?

target_item.name: Disorganized_Abnormal_Behavior
target_item.manifestation: I guess they brought me in because at the warehouse I keep doing things like freezing with my arms up by the forklift, copying the beeping sounds and hand signals, or moving boxes in strange little patterns even when everyone is yelling for me to stop.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking for clarification about the freezing movements and beeping sounds at the warehouse, which directly corresponds to the Disorganized_Abnormal_Behavior symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Um... well, I guess... I guess maybe they did say something like that. I didn't mean to make it sound like I was lying before, I just... I really want you to think I'm doing a good job. 

But, um, yeah, I suppose that's why they brought me in here. The manager and some of the guys were getting kind of upset. I guess sometimes by the forklift, I... I sort of get stuck with my arms up in the air. And I do make those beeping noises, like the truck backing up, and I copy the hand signals the drivers use. I don't really mean to be disruptive, I promise. It's just... it happens. 

And sometimes I arrange the boxes in, like, these specific little patterns instead of just stacking them how they want. Even when they're yelling at me to stop and hurry up, I just... I keep doing it. I know it probably looks really weird to them. I really try not to be a bother, though. 

I'm sorry I didn't just say that a minute ago. I just felt really embarrassed about it. I want to be a good worker and not cause problems. Is... is it okay that I told you that now? I hope you're not mad at me for not being clear right away. I'm really trying to be helpful, doctor.

doctor.intent: Determine if these behaviors are involuntary tics (F95.9) or repetitive restricted behaviors associated with autism spectrum disorder (F84.9). The key distinction is whether the patient experiences an irresistible urge or premonitory sensation before the behavior, which is characteristic of tics but not autism spectrum behaviors.
doctor.question: When you're about to freeze up with your arms in the air or make those beeping sounds, do you get any kind of warning feeling first - like an itch, a tingling, a buildup of tension, or anything uncomfortable that makes you feel like you need to do it?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about premonitory urges (a warning feeling, itch, tingling, or tension) before engaging in the abnormal behaviors (freezing, beeping). My symptom profile covers the manifestation of the abnormal behavior (S022), but does not contain information about premonitory urges or warning feelings preceding the behavior.

patient.answer:
Um... no, I don't think I feel anything like that. There's no... no itch or tingling or tension or anything. It's not like I feel uncomfortable and need to do it. It just... it just sort of happens before I even really realize I'm doing it. 

I'm really sorry, I wish I could tell you there was a warning feeling. If there was, maybe I could catch myself and stop it so I wouldn't bother my manager or the other guys at the warehouse. I really do want to just do my work normally and be a good employee. 

Is... is it bad that I don't feel it coming on? I hope I'm giving you the right information. I'm really trying to pay close attention to everything you're asking, I just... I really don't notice anything before it starts. Did... did I answer that okay?

doctor.intent: Distinguish between Stereotypic Movement Disorder (F95.9) and Autism Spectrum Disorder (F84.9) by determining if the repetitive behaviors are functionally impairing across multiple domains or primarily motor/behavioral, and to assess whether there are other core autism features like restricted interests or sensory sensitivities that weren't captured in childhood history.
doctor.question: Besides the freezing movements and beeping sounds at work, do you have any other things you really like to do over and over - like collecting things, organizing things in specific ways, or activities you get really focused on that are hard to stop once you start?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about repetitive behaviors, compulsions, or restricted interests (like collecting or organizing things in specific ways) which are often associated with Autism Spectrum Disorder or OCD. While the patient does arrange boxes in patterns (part of S022), the doctor is specifically asking about *other* things they like to do over and over (collecting, organizing, hyperfocusing). None of the symptom profiles explicitly cover other repetitive behaviors, compulsions, or restricted interests outside of the already discussed disorganized warehouse behaviors.

patient.answer:
Um... no, not really. I don't... I don't collect anything or do things over and over like that. I just like to keep things neat, you know? Like... just normal organizing. I don't get stuck doing it or anything. 

I mean, I mentioned the boxes before, but that's just because I want the warehouse to look nice and tidy for the manager. I'm not... I'm not obsessed with it or anything weird like that. I just want to do a good job. 

I really try to just go to work, do what I'm supposed to do, and then go home and relax. I don't have any strange hobbies or anything. I just try to be a normal guy. Is... is that what you were asking? I hope I'm explaining things right. I really want to make sure I'm giving you good answers.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the repetitive behaviors (freezing, beeping sounds, box arranging) are voluntary/intentional (suggesting Tic Disorder F95.9) or involuntary/automatic (suggesting Autism Spectrum Disorder F84.9). Specifically, clarify if the patient can consciously control these behaviors in the moment or if they occur without conscious volition.
doctor.question: When you're doing those things - like freezing with your arms up or making the beeping sounds - are you aware that you're doing them while they're happening, or do you only realize after someone points it out to you?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the patient's level of awareness or consciousness during the episodes of abnormal behavior (whether they realize they are doing it in the moment or only after being told). This specific detail about awareness/insight during the episodes is not covered in the symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Um... well, it's kind of hard to explain. I guess... I guess I sort of know I'm doing it while it's happening, but it's not like I'm thinking about it on purpose. It's more like... I'm just doing it, and I know I'm doing it, but I don't really think about how it looks until someone yells at me. 

I mean, I'm not totally checked out or anything like that. I'm still there. I just... I get kind of caught up in it, I suppose. But I'm definitely awake and aware. I don't want you to think I'm losing my mind or blacking out or anything scary like that. I'm just... I'm just doing my own thing for a minute. 

Is that... does that make sense? I hope I'm not making it sound worse than it is. I really am aware of my surroundings, I promise. I just want to make sure I'm giving you the right answer. Did I explain that okay?

inference.note: Ruled out F84.9 (Autism Spectrum Disorder) - patient reports normal childhood social development, normal peer relationships, no early social communication difficulties, and no restricted/repetitive interests in childhood. Current presentation is acute onset (6 months) with motor tics (freezing with arms up, mimicking hand signals) and vocal tics (beeping sounds). Patient demonstrates awareness during tics and no premonitory urge/tension, consistent with Tic Disorder rather than autism or other neurodevelopmental disorder.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient's symptoms are better characterized as motor tics (F95.1 - Chronic tic disorder) versus unspecified tic disorder (F95.9), specifically by clarifying if vocal tics are present alongside the motor tics, since chronic motor tic disorder requires motor tics only, whereas other tic presentations include vocal components
doctor.question: Besides the beeping sounds you make like the forklift - are there any other sounds or words that just come out of your mouth that you don't plan to say? Like throat clearing, grunting, or words that just pop out?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about vocal tics (throat clearing, grunting, or words popping out), which is not covered by any of my symptom profiles (S021, S022, functional impairment, duration, psychotic symptoms duration).

patient.answer:
Um... no, no other sounds. Just... just the beeping. I definitely don't grunt or clear my throat weirdly or... or blurt things out. I'm not... I'm not doing anything disruptive like that. 

I really try to keep quiet while I'm working, except for when I'm, you know, doing the forklift thing. I know it's important to be professional, even in a warehouse. I wouldn't want to make any noises that would make people uncomfortable or think I'm being rude. 

I'm pretty good at controlling what I say, I think. I don't just have words popping out. I hope... I hope that's a good thing? Like, it means I'm mostly doing okay, right? I'm really trying to give you the whole picture so you can see I'm trying my best. Is... is that the kind of answer you needed?

inference.note: Patient denies any premonitory urges, tension, or buildup before symptoms. Denies childhood onset or social difficulties in childhood. Symptoms are recent (6 months) and limited to motor behaviors (freezing, arm posturing, mimicry of forklift sounds/signals) with preserved awareness during episodes. No vocal tics beyond the forklift beeping mimicry, no other repetitive behaviors or compulsions. This presentation is most consistent with Motor Tic Disorder (F95.1) rather than Tourette's Disorder (F95.2), which requires both motor and vocal tics. The absence of premonitory urges makes F95.9 (Tic Disorder, unspecified) less likely than the more specific F95.1.

opening_question.intent: Establish rapport and identify the chief complaint that brings the patient to the clinic today
opening_question.question: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. Thank you for coming in today. What brings you to the clinic?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with motor tics (freezing with arms elevated, mimicking hand signals) and vocal tics (beeping sounds mimicking forklift noises) that began approximately 6 months ago. While the onset is later than typical for Tourette's disorder (usually childhood), the symptom pattern is consistent with Persistent (Chronic) Motor or Vocal Tic Disorder. The patient denies premonitory urges, which is atypical but not exclusionary. Childhood history is unremarkable with no prior tics or neurodevelopmental concerns. The tics are involuntary, occur without conscious planning, and persist despite social consequences. The recent onset and lack of multiple tic types makes F95.1 (Persistent Motor Tic Disorder) more likely than F95.0 (Tourette's).
